classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a salary list, return graph and grouped frequency table to critique claims; the hardest demand is recognising that a positive median return ignores the magnitude of larger losses.

content.prompt: For each of these scenarios, explain why the summary statistic is misleading.

inlines.text: How much do I get paid at this job?

inlines.text: The mean starting salary is $80,000!

spec.sourceRegion: Upper scenario, annotated salary list to the right of the two dialogue rows.
spec.description: Seven $30,000 entries followed by $430,000. An arrow identifies the first entry as you; a brace groups the following six entries as all your coworkers; an arrow identifies the last entry as CEO's son. The supplied average remains at the upper right, with Average underlined.
spec.mathematics: The eight supplied salaries total $640,000 and have mean $80,000. The brace covers rows 2–7 only.
spec.answerVisibility: The entire annotated list, including its supplied average, is permanent question evidence. Explanatory responses are separate.

inlines.text: The $430,000 outlier raises the mean to $80,000, although seven of the eight employees earn $30,000. The median, $30,000, better represents a typical starting salary.
The fourth and fifth salaries in ascending order are both $30,000.
7 workers earn $30 000; the CEO's son earns $430 000.
The mean is pulled up by that single outlier. It doesn't reflect what a typical employee earns.
The median ($30 000) would be more informative. Most starting salaries are $30 000.

spec.nativeReconstruction: Thirteen unfilled source-relative bars, gains/losses in original order, signed 10% ticks and axis arrows. Heights are schematic tracing coordinates, not newly asserted yearly data.

inlines.text: The median ignores the sizes of the other gains and losses. Several losses are much larger than the gains, so a median gain of 8% gives a misleading impression of overall performance.

There are 13 annual returns, so the median is the seventh return in ascending order. The six losses come before the seven gains; the middle return can therefore be positive even when the losses are much larger.
The median describes the middle annual return but ignores the size of the other gains and losses.
Several losses are much larger than the gains, so the median alone gives a misleading impression of performance.
Exact overall return is not given.
